collections.origin: Backed by Czech entrepreneur and philanthropist Karel Komárek, 0xCollection launched in Basel in 2023 as a new institution dedicated to developing and preserving new-media and digital art from 1960 to the present. Rather than building a museum, it operates as a touring, partnership-based platform, working with institutions such as the Kennedy Center to bring digital art into public exhibition spaces it does not own.

collections.origin: Rebecca Hoffberger founded the American Visionary Art Museum in Baltimore to give a permanent home to self-taught, untrained \"visionary\" artists largely ignored by the mainstream art world. It opened in a purpose-built building on Baltimore's Key Highway in 1995, later expanding into an adjacent former whiskey warehouse, and was designated by Congress as America's national museum and education center for this kind of art. Hoffberger stepped back from full-time directorship in 2022; the museum has had two further directors since.

In 2016 they opened a purpose-built museum in Whistler, funded by the Audain Foundation on a symbolic long-term municipal land lease, with a separate foundation still building its endowment.

Heckler dies; museum renames a gallery and its Visionary Award in her honor
Estate transfers dozens more works, bringing the cumulative total to date to roughly 150

collections.origin: A longtime American Folk Art Museum trustee, Audrey B. Heckler began collecting self-taught and Art Brut works in 1993 after spotting a poster for the Outsider Art Fair, building a holding of 700-plus works by figures like Martín Ramírez and Adolf Wölfli. She promised nearly all of it to her own museum in 2020, and her estate has continued transferring works since her 2024 death.

collections.name: Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena — Historical Art Collection
collections.founder: Institutional (Monte dei Paschi di Siena, founded 1472)

profile.structure: Corporate collection, bank-owned; separately, a philanthropic banking foundation (Fondazione MPS) spun off in 1995
profile.publicAccess: Palazzo Salimbeni (bank headquarters), by request/limited public opening; works also loaned to public exhibitions (e.g. Santa Maria della Scala)
profile.currentState: Still held and displayed by the bank in Siena; survived a 2013–2017 state bailout intact.
profile.size: Several hundred works and historical documents accumulated over more than five centuries

composition.focus: Sienese art from the Middle Ages through the 19th century, plus later acquisitions

pathwayTimeline.event: Monte dei Paschi is founded in Siena as a mount of piety, the origin of what becomes the world's oldest surviving bank
Adopts the Monte dei Paschi name; begins accumulating art and documents as an institutional holding
Fondazione Monte dei Paschi di Siena is spun off as a separate philanthropic banking foundation
The bank nearly collapses; the Italian state rescues it, taking a 68% stake — the art collection is not liquidated

collections.origin: Monte dei Paschi di Siena traces to a charitable mount of piety founded in 1472, making it the world's oldest bank still operating under its original name. It began accumulating paintings, sculpture and historical documents as an institutional holding shortly after founding, and the collection — still centered on the Sienese School — has remained with the bank through five and a half centuries, including a 2013–2017 near-failure and state bailout that did not touch the art.

Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena (Wikipedia)

collections.origin: Bank of America and its predecessor institutions built a corporate art collection of more than 30,000 works over decades. In 2008 the bank launched Art in our Communities, lending complete, curated exhibitions at no cost to museums and nonprofit galleries worldwide rather than operating a public venue of its own.

collections.origin: Sultan Sooud Al Qassemi began collecting modern and contemporary Arab art and in 2010 established the Barjeel Art Foundation in Sharjah to manage, preserve, and share it. For years the foundation operated without a museum of its own, becoming one of the most widely loaned Arab-art collections in the world. In 2026 it announced its first permanent museum, a purpose-built venue in Sharjah due to open in 2028.

collections.name: Bechtler Museum of Modern Art

In 2006 he committed the collection to the City of Charlotte, and in 2010 the Bechtler Museum of Modern Art opened in a purpose-built Mario Botta building, operated by a family foundation through a public-private partnership.

collections.origin: Betye Saar began collecting Black dolls in the late 1960s in Los Angeles, partly out of a childhood absence, growing up in the 1920s-30s without owning one. The 100-plus-doll collection, ranging from handmade rag dolls to mass-produced toys, became both source material for her assemblage art and a promised gift to The New York Historical, exhibited for her 100th birthday; she died days before the milestone.

In 2023 the university moved to sell three major American paintings, by Church, Hassam, and O'Keeffe, to fund dormitory renovations, over its founding director's objection; the museum closed in 2024 and reopened on reduced hours.

collections.origin: Charles Dee Mitchell, a Dallas art critic and curator who built his fortune through stock options earned at Half Price Books, spent decades assembling a personal collection weighted toward photography, conflict photography especially, and works on paper. He signed a bequest to the Dallas Museum of Art in 2021, four years before his death, committing both the collection and his distinctive East Dallas home; both arrived at the museum in 2026 exactly as written, with the house's sale proceeds funding a named endowment in his honor.

Rather than found a museum, Patricia Phelps de Cisneros chose deliberate dispersal, gifting works into the permanent collections of major existing institutions so that Latin American art enters the global canon.

Rather than sell or found a museum, they gave roughly 1,100 works to the National Gallery of Art from 1992 and, in 2008–09, distributed 2,500 more to one museum in each of the 50 states.

Griffin, founder of the hedge fund Citadel and one of the wealthiest people in the United States, has assembled one of the country's most valuable private art collections, from Abstract Expressionist and Pop masterworks to, most recently, an Old Master by Leonardo. He operates no museum of his own. The collection reaches the public entirely through long-term loans that follow his own moves: to the Art Institute of Chicago while he was based there, then to the Norton Museum of Art in West Palm Beach after his 2022 relocation to Florida, and in 2026 a Leonardo lent to the Metropolitan Museum of Art. topics.title: The Great Wealth Transfer and Art
topics.intro: Over the coming decades an unprecedented amount of private wealth will pass between generations. A large share of it is held by people who also own art, which puts the question of what becomes of a collection at the center of a much larger transition.

facts.label: Projected global wealth transfer over the coming decade (order of magnitude; sources and window vary)
Illustrative art-and-collectibles exposure implied under a modeled UHNW-share assumption — a Deloitte model, not a reported count
Share of inherited art that is retained rather than sold — the transition is usually about a change of hands, not a sale

sections.heading: The scale of the transition
sections.body: The wealth passing to heirs over the next decade is measured in tens of trillions of dollars, and a meaningful portion of it sits in art and collectibles. The headline figures are modeled estimates, not counts, and should be read as orders of magnitude.

sections.heading: Why ownership transition matters even without a sale
sections.body: Most inherited art is kept, not sold. That means the central event for a collection is usually a change of custody and responsibility, not a moment in the market, and it is exactly the moment that is most often unmanaged.

sections.heading: What it means for collections
sections.body: As collections change hands at scale, more families face the same set of decisions at once, with limited guidance on how others have handled them. That is the territory the Collection Index maps.

sources: Art Basel & UBS Survey of Global Collecting

topics.title: Estate Planning and Art Collections
topics.intro: Art does not move through an estate the way financial assets do. It is illiquid, taxed differently, expensive to hold, hard to divide, and often wanted by some heirs and not others. This is how that landscape works, and where it turns on professional advice.

facts.label: Federal estate & gift tax exemption per individual (2026)
Maximum federal rate on long-term gains from collectibles, vs 20% on most other assets, plus the 3.8% net investment income tax where it applies
Basis is generally stepped up to fair market value at death (IRC §1014)

sections.heading: What makes art different
sections.body: Illiquidity (a work cannot be partially sold to pay a tax bill), a higher collectibles capital-gains rate, estate-tax exposure at full value on an asset that produces no income, qualified-appraisal requirements, the cost of physical custody, and the problem that a single work cannot be divided among several heirs.

sections.heading: The decisions this forces
sections.body: Keep or sell; who receives the works; keep the collection intact or divide it; gift during life or transfer at death; give to charity and in what form; use a foundation or a trust.

sections.heading: The federal tax framework
sections.body: The 2026 federal estate and gift tax exemption is about $15M per individual with a 40% top rate; long-term gains on collectibles are taxed at a 28% federal maximum plus the 3.8% NIIT where applicable; and basis is generally stepped up to fair market value at death. Every figure here must be verified against the primary source before it is relied upon.

sections.heading: Charitable gifts of art
sections.body: A donor can generally deduct fair market value for a long-term-held work given to a public charity only if the charity's use is related to its exempt purpose (the related-use rule); deductions are capped as a share of adjusted gross income; and non-cash gifts above $5,000 require a qualified appraisal and IRS Form 8283, with high-value art reviewable by the IRS Art Advisory Panel.

sections.heading: State and other jurisdictions
sections.body: State estate and inheritance taxes vary by domicile and where works are held; a handful of states levy their own with far lower exemptions than the federal one, and other countries differ more sharply still. Specific jurisdiction pages will be added only where there is enough verified material to be useful.

sections.heading: Questions to work through
sections.body: Who legally owns the collection, and through what entity? What is the current cost basis? When was each work last appraised? Do the heirs want the collection? Would a museum accept it, and on what terms? Is the estate above or below the exemption? Gift during life or transfer at death?

sections.heading: Professional roles
sections.body: A qualified appraiser establishes value; an estate and tax attorney structures the transfer and models consequences; an accountant handles filings; an insurance specialist covers valuation, transport, and storage; an art adviser or collection manager assists with records, transactions, and institutional relationships.

sources: IRS, charitable contributions of property; Form 8283; Art Advisory Panel
